chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abdullah, from Ubeys ibn Hisham, from a man from his companions, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), who said:
A man came to him selling flour, so he said: 'Beware of cheating (ghish), for whoever cheats will be cheated in his wealth. And if he has no wealth, he will be cheated in his family.'

key_terms.أَهْلِهِ: His family (often referring to his wife or children in this context)
key_terms.الْغِشّ: Cheating, fraud, or short-changing in weight or quality during trade

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual and practical consequence of cheating in trade according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) warns a flour seller against *ghish* (deception in trade), establishing a reciprocal divine justice where the cheater is ultimately deceived. The Imam specifies that if the cheater lacks material wealth to lose, the penalty shifts to their family, highlighting the communal and familial impact of commercial dishonesty in Shia jurisprudence. This reflects the broader principle that ethical integrity in transaction is a prerequisite for spiritual and social well-being.
